question:
Twenty cubical blocks are arranged as shown. First, \(10\) are arranged in a triangular pattern; then a layer of \(6,\) arranged in a triangular pattern, is centered on the \(10;\) then a layer of \(3,\) arranged in a triangular pattern, is centered on the \(6;\) and finally one block is centered on top of the third layer. The blocks in the bottom layer are numbered \(1\) through \(10\) in some order. Each block in layers \(2,\) \(3\) and \(4\) is assigned the number which is the sum of the numbers assigned to the three blocks on which it rests. Find the smallest possible number which could be assigned to the top block.

[Figure 1](figures/1993_AMC_12_Q22_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
A bottom number may enter the top sum several times, so we first determine how many times each position contributes. Call that number the position's weight.

Start with weight \(1\) on the top block and work downward. A block's weight is passed to each of its three supporting blocks. If several blocks pass weights to the same block, add those weights. This exactly tracks the expansion of the sums: every route from a bottom block to the top contributes one copy of its number, and each route has a unique next block above it.

The three blocks just below the top each have weight \(1\). Passing these weights down gives the following triangular arrangement on the six-block layer:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
&&1&&\\
&2&&2&\\
1&&2&&1
\end{array}
\]
Passing them down once more gives the bottom weights:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
&&&1&&&\\
&&3&&3&&\\
&3&&6&&3&\\
1&&3&&3&&1
\end{array}
\]
For example, the center receives \(2+2+2=6\), each noncorner boundary position receives \(1+2=3\), and each corner receives \(1\). These account for all ten bottom positions.

To minimize the weighted sum, smaller numbers must occupy positions with larger weights. Indeed, suppose weights \(p>q\) hold labels \(x>y\). Swapping the labels decreases the sum by
\[
(px+qy)-(py+qx)=(p-q)(x-y)>0.
\]
Thus a minimum cannot contain such a pair. Put \(1\) at the center, \(2,3,4,5,6,7\) at the six positions of weight \(3\), and \(8,9,10\) at the corners. Every label is used exactly once, so this is an allowed arrangement, and the exchange argument proves that no arrangement has a smaller sum.

The smallest top number is therefore
\[
6\cdot1+3(2+3+4+5+6+7)+(8+9+10)
=6+81+27=\boxed{114},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

nodes.description: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1–100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor. For example, express 36 + 8 as 4 (9 + 2).
nodes.label: 6.NS.B.4

nodes.description: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.
nodes.label: 3.MD.C.7c

nodes.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.* Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.) *Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
nodes.label: 3.OA.B.5
